sentence: Aspirin belongs to a group of medicines called non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, or NSAIDs.
note: NHS aspirin page: aspirin is a type of medicine called an NSAID.

sentence: Taken at a low, regular dose, it is used to prevent blood clots and to lower the chance of a heart attack or stroke.
note: NHS: low, regular dose to prevent blood clots, lower chance of heart attack or stroke.

sentence: The NHS says low-dose aspirin is also used to help prevent high blood pressure in pregnancy, known as pre-eclampsia.
note: NHS: low dose can prevent high blood pressure in pregnancy (pre-eclampsia).

sentence: At higher doses, aspirin is used for short-term pain relief.
note: Search summary: higher doses are for short-term pain relief; Summary blended several pages; attributed to the NHS page whose title matches.

sentence: Doctors generally recommend low-dose aspirin for people at high risk of problems with the heart and blood vessels.
note: Summary: clinicians generally prescribe it for people at high cardiovascular risk. Summary blended several pages; attributed to the NHS page whose title matches.

sentence: Examples are people who have had a heart attack or stroke, or who have angina, which is chest pain caused by heart disease.
note: Summary: such as those who've had a heart attack or stroke, or angina caused by heart disease.

sentence: The NHS says most people aged 16 and over can take low-dose aspirin if a doctor recommends it.
note: Summary: most people aged 16 and over can take it if a doctor recommends it.

sentence: For preventing a heart attack or stroke, the NHS says people usually take it for the rest of their lives and do not stop unless a doctor tells them to.
note: Summary: usually need to take it for the rest of your life; don't stop unless doctor tells you.

sentence: The NHS says aspirin slows the blood's clotting action by making platelets less sticky.
note: Summary: slows the blood's clotting action by making platelets less sticky.

sentence: Platelets are tiny blood cells that clump together to help blood form a clot.
note: Plain textbook definition.

sentence: Clotting is a normal and useful process, but in people at risk of a heart attack or stroke, platelets can clump inside narrowed blood vessels.
note: Summary: clot-forming is normal, but platelets can clump inside narrowed vessels in people at risk. Summary blended several pages; attributed to the NHS page whose title matches.

sentence: Taking a low dose of aspirin every day helps to prevent this.
note: Summary: daily low-dose aspirin helps prevent that. Summary blended several pages; attributed to the NHS page whose title matches.

sentence: Research papers describe aspirin as permanently blocking an enzyme in platelets called COX-1, which reduces their ability to clump.
note: Summary: aspirin irreversibly inhibits COX-1, suppressing platelet aggregation (PMC paper on NSAIDs and aspirin's antiplatelet effects).

sentence: Because the body keeps making new platelets, the effect lasts until new platelets that aspirin has not touched are produced.
note: Summary: antiplatelet effects maintained until new, unacetylated platelets are produced.

sentence: MedlinePlus, a US source, says aspirin works by blocking natural substances that cause fever, pain, swelling and blood clots.
note: MedlinePlus rectal aspirin page: works by blocking natural substances that cause fever, pain, swelling and blood clots.

sentence: The NHS lists indigestion and stomach ache among the side effects of aspirin, along with bleeding more easily than usual.
note: Summary: common side effects include indigestion, stomach ache and bleeding more easily than usual.

sentence: It says indigestion that does not go away could be a sign that aspirin has caused a stomach ulcer.
note: Summary: if indigestion doesn't go away it could be a sign of a stomach ulcer, speak to your doctor.

sentence: A GP appointment is the route in that case, and the doctor may prescribe something to protect the stomach or switch to a different medicine.
note: Summary: doctor may prescribe something to protect your stomach or switch medicine. Route (GP appointment) is the site signposting rule.

sentence: The NHS says low-dose aspirin is best taken with or just after food, not on an empty stomach.
note: Summary of how-to-take page: preferably with or just after food, not on an empty stomach. Page URL not itself shown to carry it.

sentence: Serious side effects are rare and include stomach ulcers or bleeding inside the body, breathing difficulties and allergic reactions.
note: Summary: serious ones, though rare, include stomach ulcers or internal bleeding, breathing difficulties, allergic reactions.

sentence: The NHS lists blood in the pee, poo or vomit as a serious side effect, and a hospital leaflet mentions black bowel motions.
note: Summary: blood in pee, poo or vomit listed; a patient leaflet (lhch.nhs.uk) mentions black bowel motions, which is not separately cited.

sentence: Vomiting blood or passing blood in the poo calls for urgent medical help, such as NHS 111 or the GP the same day.

sentence: The NHS says to call 999 straight away for sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, very fast or difficult breathing, or a tight throat.

sentence: The NHS says low-dose aspirin may not mix well with many complementary and herbal medicines.

sentence: For example, some herbal products, such as turmeric, may raise the risk of bleeding.
